title: Debug: Every Product Vanished But The Ordered Ones
description:
Someone wants total quantity ordered **from completed orders only**, for every product — including products with zero completed-order quantity, which should show `0`. The query below runs without error, but silently drops every product that has no completed order at all. Find the bug and fix it.

Name the columns `name` and `total_qty`. Return the result in any order.
startingSql:
SELECT p.name, COALESCE(SUM(oi.quantity), 0) AS total_qty
FROM products p
LEFT JOIN order_items oi ON oi.product_id = p.id
LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.id = oi.order_id
WHERE o.status = 'completed'
GROUP BY p.id, p.name;
solutionSql:
SELECT p.name, COALESCE(SUM(oi.quantity), 0) AS total_qty
FROM products p
LEFT JOIN order_items oi ON oi.product_id = p.id
LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.id = oi.order_id AND o.status = 'completed'
GROUP BY p.id, p.name;
hint: A condition on a LEFT-joined table's column, placed in WHERE, quietly turns the join into an INNER JOIN — rows where that table has no match get NULL there, and `NULL = 'completed'` is never true. Move the condition into the join's own ON clause instead, so it only affects which orders count, not which products survive.

title: Debug: The Average Is Always A Whole Number
description:
Someone computed the average quantity per order line for each product and noticed every result came out as a suspiciously round whole number — real averages should have decimals. Find the bug and fix it.

Name the columns `product_id` and `avg_qty` (rounded to 2 decimals). Return the result in any order.
hint: SUM(quantity) and COUNT(*) are both integers, and SQLite (like most SQL engines) performs integer division when both sides are integers — truncating the decimal part entirely. Multiplying one side by 1.0 forces the whole division to happen in floating point.

title: Debug: The Sales Department Query Returns Nothing
description:
Someone wants every employee in the Sales department, but this query returns zero rows even though Sales clearly has employees. Find the bug and fix it.

Name the column `name`. Return the result in any order.
startingSql:
SELECT e.name
FROM employees e
JOIN departments d ON d.id = e.dept_id
WHERE d.name = 'sales';
solutionSql:
SELECT e.name
FROM employees e
JOIN departments d ON d.id = e.dept_id
WHERE LOWER(d.name) = 'sales';
hint: The `=` operator compares TEXT byte-for-byte by default in SQLite — 'sales' and 'Sales' are not equal. Normalize both sides (or at least the column) with LOWER() before comparing to a lowercase literal.

title: Debug: The Audit Log Is Missing An Entry
description:
This is meant to be a complete audit trail of every order line from both `source_orders` and `warehouse_orders` — every real row should show up, even if two rows happen to look identical. But a known duplicate entry in the source system isn't showing up twice in the output like it should. Find the bug and fix it.

Name the columns `order_id`, `customer_name` and `amount`. Return the result in any order.
hint: UNION always removes duplicate rows across both sides — exactly the wrong behavior for an audit log, where two identical-looking rows might be two genuinely separate events. UNION ALL keeps everything.

title: Debug: Every Employee "Shares" Their Own Salary
description:
This is meant to report employees who share their exact salary with **someone else** — but it currently returns literally every employee, even ones whose salary is completely unique in the company. Find the bug and fix it.

Name the column `name`. Return the result in any order.
hint: Without excluding the row itself, every employee's salary trivially "matches" e2 = themselves — a correlated subquery comparing a table to itself almost always needs an explicit `e2.id <> e.id` (or similar) to rule out the row matching its own reflection.

title: Debug: The Trailing Average Is Looking The Wrong Way
description:
This is meant to be a **trailing** average — for each employee (ordered by hire date), the average salary of themselves and the two people hired immediately *before* them. Instead it's using future hires that haven't happened yet from this row's point of view. Find the bug and fix it.

Name the columns `name` and `trailing_avg` (rounded to 2 decimals). Return the result in any order.
hint: "CURRENT ROW AND 2 FOLLOWING" looks ahead to hires that come later — the exact opposite of "trailing". A trailing window looks backward: PRECEDING, not FOLLOWING.

title: Debug: The Top Earner's Name Doesn't Match Their Salary
description:
This is meant to report, per department, the name and salary of that department's **top earner**. It runs without error and returns one row per department — but the name shown is often not actually the person earning that MAX salary. Find the bug and fix it.

Name the columns `department`, `top_earner` and `top_salary`. Return the result in any order.
startingSql:
SELECT d.name AS department, e.name AS top_earner, MAX(e.salary) AS top_salary
FROM departments d
JOIN employees e ON e.dept_id = d.id
GROUP BY d.id, d.name;
solutionSql:
SELECT d.name AS department, e.name AS top_earner, e.salary AS top_salary
FROM departments d
JOIN employees e ON e.dept_id = d.id
WHERE e.salary = (SELECT MAX(e2.salary) FROM employees e2 WHERE e2.dept_id = d.id);
hint: SQLite allows selecting a column that's neither aggregated nor in GROUP BY (most other databases reject this outright) — but the value you get back is from an arbitrary row in the group, not necessarily the one MAX() came from. Join back to find the actual row where salary equals the max instead.

title: Debug: Revenue Is Missing The Last Day
description:
This is meant to total revenue for every order placed **on or before** 2021-12-31. It's quietly excluding orders placed exactly on that date. Find the bug and fix it.

Name the column `total_revenue` (rounded to 2 decimals). The result is exactly one row.
startingSql:
SELECT ROUND(SUM(oi.quantity * oi.unit_price), 2) AS total_revenue
FROM orders o
JOIN order_items oi ON oi.order_id = o.id
WHERE o.order_date < '2021-12-31';
solutionSql:
SELECT ROUND(SUM(oi.quantity * oi.unit_price), 2) AS total_revenue
FROM orders o
JOIN order_items oi ON oi.order_id = o.id
WHERE o.order_date <= '2021-12-31';
hint: "On or before" means the boundary date itself should be included — that's `<=`, not `<`. A strict less-than silently drops every order dated exactly on the cutoff.

title: Debug: The Symmetric Difference Is Missing Half Its Rows
description:
This is meant to report every `order_id` out of sync between `source_orders` and `warehouse_orders`, **in either direction**. On some data it looks right, but on data where the two systems are completely disjoint, it's clearly missing rows it should report. Find the bug and fix it.

Name the column `order_id`. Return the result in any order.
hint: Chained set operators (EXCEPT, UNION, INTERSECT) evaluate strictly left-to-right at equal precedence in SQLite — `A EXCEPT B UNION C EXCEPT D` is `((A EXCEPT B) UNION C) EXCEPT D`, not two independent EXCEPTs joined by UNION. Wrap each EXCEPT as its own subquery in FROM to force the grouping you actually want.
